title: Worker admission — one weighted budget plus a structural heavy pool, or separate heavy and light counts
summary: Prior-art survey for backlog #3806: should dispatch of worker agents (review, light task, prepare, build/fix, calibration) be limited by ONE weighted budget with a weight per dispatch kind on top of the structural heavy-command pool, or by two separate counts (heavy workers, light workers)? Fork 1: Ninja (a global -j ceiling plus named pools with a depth), Gradle (--max-workers plus a shared-service maxParallelUsages), Bazel (declared per-action CPU/RAM against one scheduler), Airflow (pool_slots weights inside one shared pool) and Jenkins (Heavy Job executor weights) all use one shared budget plus a hard cap on the scarce resource; Hadoop MRv1's fixed map and reduce slots is the one documented static two-class split, and it idled one class while the other was saturated before MRv2/YARN replaced it with fungible containers. Declared weights can be wrong (Bazel's maintainers say resource modeling is inaccurate; Kubernetes ResourceQuota charges declared requests), which is why the structural pool stays. Per-kind ceilings inside the same budget (Jenkins Throttle categories, Slurm GrpTRES/MaxJobs beside TRESBillingWeights) are a real, additive extension, not a competing branch. Fork 2 (surfaced by the survey, absent from the original item): what happens at the head of the queue when the next item does not fit the remaining budget — the Go weighted semaphore documents strict FIFO to avoid starving large requests, Airflow issue #29474 is the mirror complaint, and only the exclusive (calibration) weight is unreachable under pure skip-ahead admission. Also records that the repo's heavy pool fails open after 20 minutes and is bypassable, so it is a bounded-wait guarantee, not a hard cap.
